FOR MANAGERS OF ENGINEERS · A 5-MINUTE GUIDE

Give your AI agents a shared understanding.
Then check their work.

Open Ontologies is software your engineers can use to work with explicitly defined concepts and relationships: check structured facts, answer questions, derive consequences, and preview what a definition change would affect.

Think of an agreed company glossary that software can actually use—plus tools to check whether new information follows it.

Show me an example ↓Explore the participant diagrams →

An independent learning guide to fabio-rovai/open-ontologies. The security scenario is just sample data.

01 / THREE DIFFERENT THINGS

The vocabulary, your facts, and the tool.

A

An ontology

The agreed meaning of things and how they relate.

“A person can hold a role in a particular organization.”

Your team defines the model. Public vocabularies supply reusable parts.

B

Your knowledge graph

Specific facts written using those definitions.

“Dana holds the SOC analyst role for this incident.”

The model is the structure; the graph contains your actual people, roles and events.

C

Open Ontologies

The engine that operates on that model and those facts.

“Check this new fact. Find this role. Show what this change implies.”

Your engineers integrate it into an application or an agent workflow.

“Open ontology” is a general idea; “Open Ontologies” is this particular project. Schema.org is a shared vocabulary. It is not another name for the engine.

02 / FOLLOW ONE QUESTION

“Who is the SOC analyst for this incident?”

A model could guess from a message or title. With a maintained graph, an agent can ask for the recorded assignment and its context. That only helps if the assignment is accurate and current.

Illustrative integration, not a live AI call. Time flows down; the dashed arrow is a reply. Inspect the recorded query →

What you gain

Agents can refer to the same named people, roles and incidents instead of each inventing its own interpretation. You can inspect the data used to answer.

What you still own

Engineers must connect your data, match identities, keep assignments current and enforce permissions. Passing a data check does not prove a fact is true or authorize an action.

03 / THE PRACTICAL VALUE

Four jobs you can ask the engine to do.

01

Ask precise questions

Find the person assigned to a specific role and incident, using linked facts.

↗02

Catch defined data mistakes

Flag an unknown field or a number where your rules require a name. Checks cover the rules you supplied.

↗03

Work out implied facts

If every response action is an action, a particular response action also counts as an action. This is rule-based deduction, not an AI guess.

↗04

Preview a definition change

Before changing a category, inspect which new conclusions the selected rules would produce. This is the project’s central emphasis.

↗
Why the change preview matters: A small edit to a shared definition can change the answers of several agents. Review the consequences before rolling out that definition.

04 / YOU DON’T HAVE TO NAME EVERYTHING YOURSELF

Borrow a shared vocabulary. Define your own business context.

Schema.org

Reuse terms for a person, organization, role and action. These give systems common names for common ideas.

Public vocabulary ↗

W3C PROV-O

Describe where information came from and who it is attributed to. Provenance lets you inspect a source; it does not certify that source.

Provenance vocabulary ↗

Your extensions

Add the concepts particular to your business, such as an incident assignment and the incident it belongs to. Decide what fields are required.

See how we combine them →

This lab includes selected public definitions, not all of either vocabulary. Your internal facts do not become public merely because you use public terms.

05 / CHOOSE THE JOB BEFORE THE TOOL

How does it compare?

These options overlap and can be combined. The guidance below is an architectural judgment, not a benchmark or a claim that one product wins every category.

Options for giving agents reliable context and rules
ApproachPrefer it when…Main tradeoff
Document search / RAGThe task is to find relevant passages and summarize policies or knowledge.Retrieving a passage does not itself enforce a shared model or establish that a conclusion follows. It can provide evidence for a graph.
SQL + application rules
JSON Schema for data contracts		Your records and workflows are well understood. You need ordinary data constraints and predictable business logic.Often a simpler starting point. Cross-system meaning and deductions must be modeled in tables, queries or code; they are possible, not automatic.
Graph database
Example: Neo4j		Exploring and querying networks of relationships is central to the product.A property graph gives you connected data. Shared ontology meaning, inference and change review require explicit design and suitable tooling.
RDF / ontology stack
Example: Apache Jena		You need standards-based linked data and reasoning, and want to assemble the capabilities around your platform.A close alternative: Jena provides inference and rule engines. Compare supported rules, deployment fit and the review workflow your team would have to build.
Open OntologiesYou want an ontology engine with a focused workflow for inspecting the consequences of changes.You take on modeling and integration work. Validate the exact release, rule coverage, performance and operational fit with your own data.

06 / THE MANAGEMENT DECISION

Useful discipline. Real maintenance cost.

Reasons to consider it

  • Several agents or systems need consistent definitions.
  • You need to inspect why a result follows from supplied facts and rules.
  • Definition changes can affect many downstream answers.
  • Public terms could reduce bespoke mappings between teams.

Costs and limitations

  • People must agree on definitions—and own updates.
  • Connecting messy data and resolving identities takes work.
  • Wrong or stale inputs can yield wrong but internally consistent answers.
  • Coverage and performance depend on the rules, engine version and data.
  • Authentication, approvals and actual tool execution remain application responsibilities.
Does a “proof” mean the AI’s answer is true?

No. A proof can establish that a conclusion follows from specified premises under supported rules. It cannot establish that your source data is accurate or complete. The project offers certificate workflows; this lab generated a certificate, but its independent checker failed to start, so we do not claim independent verification.

Is this a replacement for our LLM or agent framework?

No. An LLM can interpret language and propose structured facts; your application can send those facts for checks and queries. Your agent framework still coordinates tasks and tool calls. This site illustrates that integration and replays engine results; it does not run an LLM.

When is it probably unnecessary?

If one agent only summarizes documents, start with document retrieval and answer evaluation. If a few structured fields and straightforward rules solve the problem, a database and schema validator may be enough. Add ontology tooling when shared meaning and rule consequences are an actual source of errors or maintenance cost.

07 / A SMALL FIRST EXPERIMENT

Ask your engineers to prove one benefit.

Choose one question that agents currently answer inconsistently. Model only the concepts needed for it, connect a small verified dataset, and compare against your current approach.

  1. Agree on the answer. Write expected answers, including “we don’t know,” with a domain expert.
  2. Test failure cases. Try an invented field, a wrong value type, stale data and a misleading definition change.
  3. Measure the tradeoff. Compare answer correctness, explanation quality, latency, and engineering effort to maintain the model.

Continue if the reduction in mistakes and review effort justifies the ongoing modeling cost. This is a suggested evaluation, not a measured ROI claim.
